title: Ranbir Said No. Imran Said No. Saif Ali Khan Said 'Okay, Chal' — and Walked Into a Classic.
excerpt: As Cocktail 2 fills theatres, Saif reveals the dirty little secret of the 2012 original: nobody wanted to share the screen with Deepika's Veronica. Their loss became his legend.
body:
There is a particular kind of Bollywood story that only gets told once the statute of limitations on ego runs out. Fourteen years, in this case. The film is a certified classic, the careers are secure, the wounds have healed, and an actor can finally lean back and laugh about the role half the industry passed on before it landed in his lap.

Saif Ali Khan is in exactly that chair. With Cocktail 2 now playing to packed weekend houses — Shahid Kapoor's rom-com cleared a reported ₹44 crore in its opening weekend — the original Cocktail has come roaring back into the conversation. And in a freewheeling sit-down with Variety India, Saif pulled the curtain back on a casting saga that, frankly, sounds more delicious than the film itself.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=MPVZwSagCk8

Here is the secret nobody told you in 2012: Saif was not the first choice to play Gautam. He wasn't the second, either.

!Shahid Kapoor — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

""I remember some names they asked," he recalled."
"They had Deepika and Diana, but they couldn't get a hero to play the part, probably because Veronica's part is so delicious." — Saif Ali Khan, to Variety India

Sit with that for a second. Deepika Padukone and Diana Penty were locked. The leading ladies were in place. And the male lead — the supposed centre of gravity for a Hindi film of that era — was a revolving door of polite refusals. According to Saif, the script made the rounds to some of the biggest young heartthrobs of the moment before it ever reached him.

"I remember some names they asked," he recalled. "I think they had asked Imran Khan and they had asked Ranbir Kapoor. And they had asked a few people, and I said, 'Okay, chal, I'll do it.'"

Okay, chal. Two words, tossed off like a man agreeing to grab dinner. That casual shrug is how Saif walked into one of the defining rom-coms of his generation.

!Variety India — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The reason the boys hesitated is the most telling part of the whole story, and it doubles as a backhanded compliment to Padukone. Veronica — the wild, vulnerable, free-spirited disco-throb who falls apart so beautifully — was written to dominate. She was the part with the fireworks. Gautam, the flirt caught between Veronica's chaos and Meera's calm, risked being furniture next to her. The young stars of 2012, calculating their screen-time math, blinked. Saif, secure and a little older, didn't.

And he has the receipts. "I think they should all be very thankful I did," he said, with the kind of theatrical humility that only a Nawab can pull off. "That's my story. Yeah, because I had great fun. I love Homi. And we had a good time doing it."

The Homi in question is Homi Adajania, the director who had earlier coaxed Saif through the quirky Being Cyrus (2005) and who, in a neat full-circle move, is back behind the camera for Cocktail 2. The bond clearly held. Saif brought a mature, rueful vulnerability to Gautam that a fresher face might have flattened into a himbo — and the film became one of the year's biggest money-spinners, propelled by a soundtrack that still detonates at every desi wedding from New Jersey to Wembley.

There's a richer footnote, too. By one account, Ranbir didn't just decline the role himself — he reportedly advised Deepika against doing the film at all. She ignored him, trusted her gut, and delivered one of the finest performances of her career. Ranbir, to his credit, is said to have later conceded his judgment was off. It's the rare casting misfire where everyone involved eventually agrees the universe arranged itself correctly.

That's the quiet thrill of Saif's confession landing exactly as Cocktail 2 mints money. The sequel — a "spiritual successor" more than a direct continuation — hands the baton to Shahid Kapoor, Kriti Sanon and Rashmika Mandanna, with Adajania once again steering the emotional chaos. For the diaspora, both films are an easy stream: the 2012 original lives on Netflix and Prime Video across most US, UK and Canada regions, perfect homework before the sequel hits screens overseas through the usual desi-cinema distributors.

Watch them back to back and Saif's point makes itself. The hero everyone was scared to play turned out to be the easiest one to love — and the man who shrugged 'okay, chal' got to keep the legend. Somewhere, two A-listers are still thinking about the one that got away.
